title: CRUSHING the Sicilian with the Alapin | Amazing Checkmate!! | GM Naroditsky's Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: We roll out the Alapin — e4, and Black answers with the Sicilian, c5.
The Alapin move: c3, preparing to build a big centre with d4.
Black develops the knight to f6, hitting e4, so we shove it away with e5.
The knight jumps in to d5.
Here the traditional move is d4, but the newer idea — the one I like at this level — is the knight to f3 first.
Black plays d6, striking at our e5 pawn.
Now the modern idea from the Alapin course — a check on b5. To feel its power you need one very important tactic in this line.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7 — the most popular response, and exactly what we wanted to provoke.
We drop the bishop back to c4. The point: if the knight retreats to b6, hitting the bishop, we have a trick.
Black plays the natural knight to b6, attacking our bishop — and now the trick.

We sacrifice — the bishop takes on f7 with check, and the king must recapture on f7. Most people follow with the knight to g5, but here that's WRONG: the king to g8 is a dead end, and the queen to b3 isn't mate because Black blocks with c4.

The key is to start with e6, check. If you play the knight to g5 first, e6 lets the bishop retreat to e8. So e6 first: if Black takes with the king, it's forced mate with the knight to g5, the king driven into the open; if Black takes with the bishop, the knight to g5 wins the piece back with a slight edge.
This isn't a forced win, just a small edge — and Black takes with the bishop, capturing on e6.
Now the knight to g5, check.

Black's king steps to f6 — this is supposed to be losing. I'm nearly certain it's the queen to f3. Calculating: if the king takes the knight, then h4, the king to g6, h5, the king to h6 forced, then d4 with a discovery — but the king can escape to g7. Instead, after h4 and the king to the side, the queen to e3 is mate. d4 would let Black save the bishop to d5 and make our queen harder to activate.
So the queen to f3, check — I still remember this is the move.
Black takes the knight, capturing on g5 — if I've calculated right, it's forced mate.
h4, check.
The king to h6 — and what Black forgot is the queen-f4 idea.
The queen to f4, check — and it's mate, with just a pawn, the queen and the rook. A thirteen-move game, all theory, and Black resigns.
This is the power of the Alapin — a misrepresented opening. It's painted as a dry, low-key positional anti-Sicilian, but in its modern treatment you get sharp tactical lines like this one.

Originally the Alapin was played very positionally, but new discoveries have turned it into an exciting tactical opening — which is why I play it almost exclusively in blitz, along with the knight-f3, d6, bishop-b5-check setup.
Since that was only a short game, let's use it to go through some theory.
The speedrun is about openings, so this is the perfect chance. First important point after the knight reaches d5.
Notice I played the knight to f3. The old-school move is to play d4 immediately.
You might think there's no difference, because after c takes d4...
...White typically plays the knight to f3 anyway.
...and note that d takes c3 isn't possible for Black.
So after the knight to f3, Black plays either the knight to c6 or d6, usually the knight to c6.
And you reach the old main line — c takes d4, d6, the bishop to c4.
...the old main line.

Now Black has d takes c5, which equalises, but the knight to b6 is the most popular move — and the same f7 trick does NOT work here, because Black's bishop is still undeveloped, which paradoxically favours Black.
The bishop develops to c4.
...the knight to b6.
Here Black doesn't have to take the pawn — with the bishop still home, Black just drops the king back to g8, and we have no bishop left to capture with.
So the king to g8 defuses it in that move order.
So there most people play the bishop to b5.
The bishop to b5 — then d takes e5, the bishop to d7 — all very old theory.
...d takes e5, the knight recaptures on e5, the bishop to d7.
The knight takes on d7, the queen recaptures.
The knight to c3, e6...
...castles, and in this position Black used to play automatically.
Black traditionally played the bishop to e7 automatically. Do you know White's most challenging move — the one giving a small but nagging edge?
If Black is allowed the bishop to b7, the line is perfectly fine for Black — but the queen to g4 is the accurate move, keeping the edge.
Black castles kingside, and here's another important point.
If you excitedly play the bishop to h6...
...it's a blunder, because Black plays the queen takes d4 — the knight defends the queen, the queen defends the pawn, and White's queen hangs.
So you must start with the bishop takes c6 — a move people forget: take the knight FIRST.
The bishop takes on c6...
...Black typically recaptures with the pawn, though the queen also works; then White plays the bishop to h6.
The bishop to h6.
...forcing the bishop to f6.
Now the rook to d1, essentially pre-moving the knight to e4.
Even if Black steps the king away from the pin...

...you can still play the knight to e4. This has happened hundreds of times over the board — and if Black takes the bishop, you take back and ruin Black's pawn structure, with a small but stable edge.
Stockfish likes White by about a third of a pawn — a comfortable line. Unfortunately, in the last decade computers have shown the bishop to b7 isn't forced.
...there are better moves that equalise immediately.
The most incisive is just a6, forcing White's hand at once.
White typically takes on c6...
...Black recaptures with the queen, and by delaying the bishop's development takes the sting out of the queen-g4 idea.
White usually plays the bishop to e3.
Black centralises the knight to d5 — dead equal; White isn't worse, but has no advantage.
The rook to c1, the bishop to b7 — and if you play the queen to g4...
...the queen to g4...
...Black can eliminate the bishop: the bishop trade before castling, f takes e3, castles...
...and Black is completely fine, just equal.
At a lower level, though, this old line is very good, because many people still don't know the theory...
...they'll stumble as early as this position.
They'll play something odd, or...
...in this position...
...they'll play e6, a viable alternative that transposes into a line very promising for White.
...very promising for White.
But at the higher level we're at...
...I like the newer move.
Not the newest course move exactly, but the newer move...
...which is the knight to f3.
The idea: our opponent played d6, a different line, but if Black plays the knight to c6...
...you immediately play the bishop to c4, skipping d4 entirely.
Now if Black plays e6...
...you play d4, and generally transpose to a promising line we just saw via the other move order.
...via the other move order.

If Black drops back to b6, we drop back to b3 — a more tactical, more theoretical, very promising position. Black has two main moves here: c4, natural, preventing d4; and d6 or d5, essentially the same, playing the d-pawn and then the queen takes d6, you castle. One amateur trap: if Black plays the bishop to g4, even grandmasters miss the classic bishop-takes-f7 and knight-to-g5. The main move is the bishop to b6, trading the light bishops — and about a year ago a new idea completely rejuvenated the line. The old view was dead equal: White played d4 automatically, trades, a draw. But the a4 idea was found, and Black's been in significant trouble since. The plan is simple: drive the pawn up to a6, provoking weaknesses on Black's queenside. Black steps the queen away to prepare e6, White pushes a5, Black centralises the knight, White pushes a6, and ONLY now d4 — a big central initiative. The queen aims at g7, making the kingside hard to develop; the knight comes to c4, sometimes the pawn to c4, the rook to d1. If Black pushes c4, again Black can play d6 and White pushes a4 with the knight to a3, standard Alapin; or Black goes after the pawn with the queen to c7, and the new idea is to just sacrifice the pawn and castle. If Black accepts, you get White's "potential energy" — down a pawn and barely developed, yet plus one, because once you push d3 everything comes alive: the bishops aim at the kingside, the rook comes to e1 with tempo, and a5 knocks the knight to an awkward square. After the queen to c7, the knight to a3 aims for b5, sacrificing another pawn; open with d3, the c4-pawn hangs, and after the queen takes e3 it's over. If Black plays e6 there's a tactic: the knight to b5, the queen takes a1, the knight to c7, the king to d8 — and here the high-level detail: everyone under 2000 plays the bishop to g5 automatically, but Black plays the king takes c7 and escapes; White probably wins but unconvincingly. The stronger player desperados the knight, takes the e6 pawn FIRST, and only THEN the bishop — and that pawn makes all the difference: e6 becomes a huge target, Black lacks structural integrity, and it's plus five. The lesson: always pause before an automatic, non-forced move to see if you can improve the tactic — the difference between clearly better and completely winning.
I had an over-the-board game against a Chinese grandmaster in this line — d6, takes, takes, castles, the bishop to g4, the rook to e1 — another line to explore where White is quite a bit better.
So those are Black's options after the bishop to c4. Our opponent played a different line — the immediate d6.
The immediate d6, and here again a new idea.
The check on b5 that looks superficial but carries a deep idea — you provoke the bishop to d7, then drop back to c4.
You provoke the bishop to d7...
...and drop back to c4. Why not the bishop to c4 immediately?
Because Black can step back to b6, and then the f7 trick doesn't work — Black just ducks to g8.
So the check first provokes the bishop to d7, THEN you drop to c4.
What if Black doesn't play the bishop to d7? The only other move is the knight to c6 — the knight to d7 is too awkward, nobody plays it.
If Black plays the knight to c6...
...the knight to c6...
...you castle — again the theme of delaying d4 until the right moment — and Black is in trouble.
If Black plays the bishop to d7 now...
...it is finally time for d4, and Black position collapses — the offside knight is vulnerable, the kingside undeveloped.
If Black takes on d4...
...you push c4, a weird idea, forcing the knight back.
The knight to c7, takes, takes...
...e takes d6, recapture...
...develop with tempo, the bishop to g5.
The bishop to e7 — the line in my file.

You take on c6 first, then trade, the rook to e1, the knight to e6, the knight to d4, and White is clearly better — much better than the greedy knight to f5, which forgets that after the queen to f6 Black counterattacks b2. Prioritise development; White is clearly better with Black saddled by two weaknesses.
This shows that above 2000, learning openings is glamorised but it's really at least 75% going through and memorising these variations and understanding them.
To help memorise, use memory markers — remember the unusual ideas. Here the unusual idea is that when Black plays c takes d4, you push c4 — you rarely see that in the Alapin.
So tell yourself: in this line, remember to push c4.
And tell yourself: because of the bishop-takes-f7 trick, I have to provoke the bishop to d7...
...which is why I give this check first.
So the bishop to d7, the bishop to c4, the knight to b6...
...the bishop to c4...
...and the knight to b6...
...is a mistake.
The best move is e6 — the way for Black to equalise, though it still leads to an exciting position where White has practical pressure.
The move is d4, and after c takes d4...
...you can do several things.
One interesting idea is to castle kingside.
If Black keeps eating pawns with d takes c3...
...you take the knight, the bishop takes d5...
...e takes d5...
...the knight recaptures on c3, with a huge development lead and Black's centre collapsing.
This is how you play the Alapin now — ignore all of Black's hanging pawns, prioritise development.
The bishop to g5...
...and if Black plays f6, White has a crushing blow.
The knight takes e5 — both pieces hanging, but Black can only take the bishop.
...f takes g5, the queen to h5, check.
...g6, and you don't take the rook — the knight takes on g6.
...h takes g6...
...the queen takes g6 with check, the king to e7, and the knight takes d5 is mate.
That's the idea — prioritising development. So d takes e3, you take the bishop, take the knight.
If Black takes the pawn, the line is equal but dangerous for Black.
You play the knight takes pawn...
...and if Black plays pawn takes pawn...
...you take twice on d5, with a big double attack on those two pawns.
So Black has to know the move knight to b6...
...the knight to b6 — not an easy move, stepping back.
Stepping back to b6...
...you play Smith-Morra style — drop your bishop back and say, take my c3 pawn.
The bishop to b3.
But here...
...you throw in the queen to h5 with a huge initiative.
Black plays g6...
...the queen steps back to f3, never afraid of Black grabbing your queenside pawns — that's beside the point.
Really good line — this bishop-b5 check is very problematic.
Black can equalise with careful play...
...but below 2500 it's super challenging — which is why I recommend the Alapin to lower-rated players.
So the knight to b6...
...and now the bishop-f7 and e6 trick — our opponent played the bishop takes c6, letting us show the forced mate.

The relative lesser evil — funnily the computer calls this equal, but we'll get to that. Many get scared and play the king to g8, understandable but terrible for Black: the queen takes d7, you castle; if the knight to c6, push a4 again — if Black plays a5 you fork and win the knight; if e6, push d4, take, take, then the knight to c3, a5, the rook to e1, and Black's position is visually terrible.

The only testing try is to take the pawn; Black can also take with the king, transposing to the game — the knight to g5, the queen to f3, and if the king takes on g5 he's mated, but you must know one very important move that forces mate, and it's NOT h4 — it's the queen to f7. This restricting move is the hardest to find in a king hunt: you're tempted to spray checks, but restricting moves set up the mating net far better. If you play d4 and get excited about the discovery, the attack fizzles and the king runs to g6. You have to block the escape to f7. Then if the king steps back to h6, d4 and h4, and h takes g5 is mate next move. This reminds me of a famous Petrosian combination: white to play, the queen takes f6 with check, the king takes f6, the bishop to e5 with check, the king to g5 — the instructive position. Newer players want h4, a bad move that HELPS the king escape, same with f4, same with the rook to h4, which Black blocks with h5. The correct move is the quiet bishop to g7, restricting escape squares — hard to find because you're down a queen and want to rush, but the king's in no danger, so there's no hurry. The bishop to g7 forces mate in two or three. The point: in a king hunt, don't rush the obvious checks — first identify the escape routes and find a slow restrictive move that sets the mating net, like the queen to f7 in our game. Then the queen to f7, and now d4 is fine; the computer line is g6 check, d3 or d4, then h3 setting up g4, another quiet move, check, the knight to d2 heading to f3 — mate in two, the pieces cooperating beautifully. That's why Black has to play the bishop to f5. Remember where this came from — the king takes c6; our opponent played the bishop to b6, but we could reach the same via the bishop to f5. The computer calls it equal, massively misleading: after White plays g4, Black faces an incredibly difficult defensive task and must play ultra-accurately — e6 to meet the mate-in-one threat and defend the bishop, then White's knight to e4 check forcing the king to e7 (the king to f7 is much worse — you take and have the queen to h5 with check), then g takes f5, which looks terrible but after e f5, the queen to f5, the queen to d7, White's attack rolls on; you drop the queen back, Black plays the knight to c6, you play d4 opening the bishop, and only super-accurate play with c d holds — you're not supposed to check with the bishop to g5, you recapture. It's enough to remember: give the check, meet the bishop to f5 with g4, remember the knight to e4. If Black plays g6 instead it's losing — after g f, g f, the queen to h5 comes to f7 unstoppably.

Our opponent played the king to h6 — and again d4 is very bad: Black plays g5 and the king escapes to g7. So the correct move is the queen to f4, mate in one. This strong player just didn't know the line, figured I was bluffing, went for it too fast, and got mated — that's the benefit of learning a course: you win countless games like this.
A short game, but hopefully a semi-instructive theory session.
Hopefully you found it instructive.

The Alapin is far more practical to learn in a couple of weeks, with the aid of the speedrun. That's where we'll end.
